title: v1 ships server-sent events. On the same HTTP API, the same port, the same OpenAPI document, and the same token rule.
Resumption is the Last-Event-ID header carrying the change cursor.
WebSockets are refused for v1 on the recorded evidence: bidirectionality buys nothing when every mutation is already a REST call, the protocol carries no cursor to resume from...
The stream carries notifications, not projections.
state: sent once when the stream opens and carrying the current cursor
changed: sent as stored records change and carrying the cursor
notice: carrying a notice's identifier, type, and level, so a consumer can decide whether it deserves the operating system's attention
Every list, forecast, and review is still read over REST.
On reconnect the client compares the state cursor with its own and refetches over REST when they differ...
There is no replay buffer and no race between a replay finishing and the live tail starting.
One Java reader lives in the module that holds the remote proxy and serves the desktop, tray, and command line clients.
It parses the stream, resends the cursor as Last-Event-ID, and backs off on failure.
Plain polling stays available as a fallback, because a dropped stream is a latency problem rather than a correctness problem.
A comment heartbeat every fifteen seconds, which survives the sixty-second default idle read timeout of a default nginx proxy...
A server-side emitter timeout of thirty minutes, so a connection is recycled through the deliberate reconnect path instead of living for days.
The event id is the change cursor, so the standard resume mechanism does the work the project already needed a cursor for.
The response is declared as text/event-stream with an explicit event schema, which OpenAPI 3.1 expresses as one payload schema.
When the pinned springdoc line emits OpenAPI 3.2, the endpoint gains itemSchema so each event in the stream is described independently.
child-efforts: the API child owns the stream endpoint and the event schema
child-efforts: the module holding the remote proxy owns the reader; the desktop, tray, and command line clients consume it.
decisions-agent-interface: MCP is unchanged, since the agent surface stays tools over stdio; an agent that wants push reads the API stream like any other consumer.
decisions-forecast-warnings: the notice event carries type and level, so an external consumer applies the same level-based judgement the product applies.
decisions-data-lifecycle: the cursor is a log position, so resumption reads the log the project already keeps; the stream adds no storage of its own.
release-plan: the stream lands with the daemon stage, because that is when the API exists.
